# Education in New Zealand
Education in New Zealand has its origins in Māori traditional knowledge transmission through elders (tohunga) before European arrival. European-style formal schooling began in 1815 with missionary-established schools teaching in the Māori language, evolving into a free, compulsory, secular national system by 1878. Early childhood education includes center-based (kindergarten, licensed centers) and parent-led services, all licensed by the Ministry of Education. Primary education spans Years 1–8, with Years 7 and 8 sometimes at separate intermediate schools; secondary education covers Years 9–13. Schooling is free and compulsory for children aged 6–16, with most starting at age 5 and continuing to about 17. Families may home-school with approval. The school year runs late January to mid-December, divided into four terms.
The national curriculum is compulsory for state and state-integrated schools and includes eight learning areas such as English or Māori language, mathematics, arts, health, science, social sciences, technology, and languages. From Year 11, students work toward the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA), with options like Cambridge or International Baccalaureate offered. Schools are categorized as state schools (fully funded and secular), state-integrated schools (funded but retain special character like religion), and private schools (mainly funded by fees). Funding mechanisms consider socio-economic deciles with higher support for lower-decile (poorer) schools. Māori education has seen revitalization through immersion schools (kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa Māori), contributing to improved academic outcomes for Māori students relative to mainstream settings. Special education and home-schooling are supported with specific provisions. Despite New Zealand’s reputation as having a strong education system, international assessments have identified challenges in mathematics performance, prompting ongoing curriculum and teaching reviews.
